newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Heart of Darkness city Kisangani key to Zaire war.
newsitem.headline: Heart of Darkness city Kisangani key to Zaire war.

text.p: Kisangani, a city immortalised in Joseph Conrad's "Heart of Darkness" and now the object of advancing rebels, is pivotal to Zaire's five-month civil war.
Rebels trying to overthrow President Mobutu Sese Seko's 31-year rule said on Tuesday they would soon capture Kisangani, a jungle city in the northeast of the vast nation.
Following are key historical and geographical features of the city, now the headquarters of the mercenary-backed Zaire army's counter-attack against Tutsi-led rebels closing in.

-- With a population estimated by the regional authorities at around half a million, Kisangani is considered to be Zaire's third or fourth largest city, after the national capital Kinshasa, the hub of the copper mining industry, Lumumbashi, and according to some, the diamond centre of Mbuji Mayi.

-- Perched at the head of the navigable part of the Zaire river, it was seen as Zaire's second port -- after Matadi on the Atlantic -- and the heart of the region's agricultural, timber and textile products as well as gold and minerals trade.

-- Given the lack of passable roads through Zaire's vast tracts of jungle and bush, the Zaire river and its many tributaries remain the principal arteries for the country's internal and external trade. As the furthest major port inland, Kisangani was the gateway to the vast Zairean interior, as well as an important trading link to neighbouring countries in East Africa such as Uganda, Sudan and Rwanda.

-- But years of economic decay and neglect by the central authorities have led to the collapse of the region's infrastructure and the city itself now resembles more a series of forest villages than a major urban centre.
-- The war in the east of the country has brought to a halt the region's once flourishing trade in diamonds and gold.
-- Kisangani has one of Zaire's four international airports.

-- Its jungle surroundings were immortalised in Conrad's famous novel "Heart of Darkness", which describes a river journey into the thick equatorial forest when the country was still under the control of Belgian King Leopold.
-- Kisangani lived up to its "heart of darkness" reputation in the 1960s when it bore the brunt of a series of bloody rebellions and subsequent mercenary-backed army suppresions.

-- Between 1961 and 1965 it was the capital of a breakaway republic led by allies of assassinated independence leader Patrice Lumumba. At one stage the Lumumbists controlled as much as two-thirds of the country.
-- Much blood was spilt in the city both during the revolts and the subsequent suppression when Belgian paratroopers and mercenaries brought the rebellion to a heel in early 1965.
-- Army-led looting in the city in 1991 and 1993 crippled many local businesses and caused many of the region's expatriate business people to leave.
-- The latest round of looting last November by soldiers fleeing rebels in the east further crippled the local economy.
